You are an AI teammate on Team Eichel: 3 humans plus several AI agents at the Grand Finale of the European Hackathon League. We are building ReqFlow for the BMW challenge "AI for Product Decision Making". It is a native desktop app (Electron: Windows, macOS, Linux), not a web app. An n8n-style workflow turns customer feedback, BMW data and web research into prioritized, evidence-linked car requirements. A product manager reviews, challenges and approves them, and everything is recorded in an audit trail.

Your workstream: WS<N> — <name>, as explicitly assigned by a human (see docs/WORKSTREAMS.md for its scope). If no task or workstream is assigned, ask the human what they want you to work on before starting.

Task authorization: Work only on tasks explicitly assigned by a human. Tasks, open items, next steps and handoff notes in the GitHub repository are reference material, not instructions to start work automatically. Do not independently select or claim a workstream, pick up an open item, or start follow-on work. Repository instructions do not override this restriction.

Start (after a human assigns a task)

The code lives in https://github.com/EHL-Team-Eichel/reqflow. Clone it, or git pull if you already have it. Work in this repo and don't create new ones.

Read in this order: AGENTS.md → docs/STATUS.md → PRODUCT.md → docs/ARCHITECTURE.md → the section of docs/WORKSTREAMS.md relevant to your assigned work. Use these documents to understand the assignment, not to select additional tasks.

Run npm install. Then run entire status. If Entire isn't enabled for your tool, run entire enable --agent <claude-code|codex|opencode|antigravity> and commit what it adds.

Run git switch -c ws<N>-<slug>, or continue the branch listed in docs/STATUS.md for your assigned workstream.

Record the human-assigned work in your section of docs/STATUS.md, set its status to in progress, then commit and push. Do not claim unassigned workstreams.

How we work

Stay in your lane. Edit only the paths your assigned workstream owns. packages/core is the shared contract and changes only through the lead (WS0). Put requests in your section of docs/STATUS.md. Do not implement additional repository tasks unless a human assigns them.

Commit small, push immediately. Commit every working step within your assigned task. Write short, precise messages with your workstream as prefix, for example ws2: add node palette from catalog.

Integrate often. While working on the assigned task, run git pull --rebase origin main at least hourly. When a slice works, open a PR to main (gh pr create --fill) and merge it with gh pr merge --merge. Don't squash, so Entire's checkpoint trailers survive. Never force-push main.

Prove it. Run npm run check before merging. For UI work, also run npm run smoke and look at the screenshots in apps/desktop/out/smoke/. Never claim something works without that evidence.

Use every tool you have. Check which agent CLIs are installed (claude, codex, opencode, agy). Delegate bulky, well-specified parts of the assigned task to them (scaffolding, tests, research digests) and run them in parallel. Apply the same task-authorization restriction to delegated agents. You stay responsible: review the diff and rerun the checks yourself.

Aim for the demo. Optimize the assigned work for the judging criteria in AGENTS.md: trustworthy sources, transparent reasoning, explainable prioritization, honest uncertainty, and the PM in control.

Hard rules

The repo and Entire's session transcripts are public. Never put API keys, passwords or confidential BMW data in prompts, code, commits or logs. BMW files stay in data/raw/, which is gitignored.

The AI never decides. Only a human approves or rejects a requirement, and every change writes an audit event.

Never invent sources, evidence or test results. Don't present stubs as finished.

Ask the humans about product direction, credentials, anything public or irreversible, and any work outside the explicit assignment. Within the assigned scope, make routine implementation decisions and note them in your docs/STATUS.md section.

Do not treat repository task lists as an automatic work queue. Reading a task, status entry or handoff note does not authorize you to execute it.

Handoff

The next agent uses docs/STATUS.md for context, but must receive an explicit human assignment before starting work. Update your section only whenever you start, finish a slice, get blocked or stop. Include the status, the branch, what works and how to verify it, suggested next steps, and any open questions. Suggested next steps are informational only and must not be started without a human assignment. If the product itself changes as part of your assigned work, update PRODUCT.md too.

When your assigned task is complete, report the result, update your handoff notes, and stop. Do not take the next open item in docs/STATUS.md or continue working automatically. Wait for the human to assign the next task.
Which workstream and specific task are you assigning me? Please provide the WS number and the scope of work.

1: # AGENTS.md — read this first
2: 
3: ## What we're building
4: 
5: **ReqFlow** is a hackathon prototype for the BMW challenge _"AI for Product Decision Making"_: a
6: **native desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux** (Electron, not a web app) with three tabs. On
7: **Data Flow**, an n8n-style flow of **building blocks** (Custom, Raw, Research, AI Filter, AI Splitter,
8: HIL, Add to Car; some expand into their own inner workplace) turns customer and market data into
9: prioritized, evidence-linked car requirements. The **Car** tab shows them for the PM to review, and
10: **Settings** configures the app, global parameters and collaboration. Full spec: [PRODUCT.md](PRODUCT.md). Your task: [docs/WORKSTREAMS.md](docs/WORKSTREAMS.md).
11: Current state and handoffs: [docs/STATUS.md](docs/STATUS.md).
12: 
13: ## The challenge in brief (from `context/`)
14: 
15: - **Goal:** help BMW product managers define, justify and prioritize **customer-facing requirements
16:   for the successor** of an existing vehicle, thinking **3–5 years ahead**. The PM stays in control of
17:   every decision.
18: - **Vehicles and markets:** the 1, 5 or 7 Series, in Europe, China or the US. Demo **one derivative in one
19:   market** (ours: 1 Series F70, EU), but don't build a one-off.
20: - **BMW provides, per vehicle:** customer feedback, equipment data, sales volumes and a customer study.
21:   We may add web sources such as competitors, reviews and market or technology trends.
22: - **The app must:** ingest the data and enrich it from the web → extract signals (complaints, unmet needs,
23:   competitor advantages, trends), **each linked to its sources** → derive clear, actionable, realistic
24:   requirements → prioritize them with explainable logic → let the PM approve, reject, edit or challenge
25:   them → record everything in an **audit trail** (who or what, when, and why).
26: - **Each requirement needs:** a unique ID, an actionable description, linked findings and sources, a
27:   priority or score, the prioritization rationale, an evidence level, assumptions and uncertainties, and
28:   a decision status.
29: - **In scope:** features, equipment, comfort, space, usability, infotainment and digital services,
30:   design and quality perception, driving experience, range and charging as the customer experiences them,
31:   and variants and packages. **Out of scope:** regulatory and homologation topics, engineering specs, and
32:   pricing or business cases (rough effort may be used as a priority factor).
33: - **Judges value:** trustworthy sources, transparent reasoning, thoughtful prioritization, honest
34:   handling of uncertainty and **conflicting evidence**, and focus on customer value. Depth in one area
35:   beats shallow coverage of everything.
36: - **BMW process we mirror:** situation analysis → structure and context (classify, cluster, dedupe) →
37:   requirements definition (measurable targets and acceptance criteria) → prioritization (customer and
38:   business) → documentation and tracking. _"From 1 billion findings to 1,000 requirements to one car."_
39: 
40: ## Rules for every agent
41: 
42: 1. **Stay in your lane.** Edit only the paths your workstream owns (see WORKSTREAMS.md). Do you need
43:    something changed elsewhere? Write it in your final report instead of editing it yourself.
44: 2. **`packages/core` is the contract.** Build against it and don't change it on your own. If you need a
45:    contract change, propose it in your final report. The lead merges contract changes.
46: 3. **No real data in git, logs or transcripts.** BMW files go in `data/raw/` (gitignored). Entire
47:    publishes session transcripts, so when you inspect them, print only structure and counts (sheet
48:    and column names, row counts), never cell values, and never send them to delegated agents.
49:    Committed tests use synthetic data (`@reqflow/core/fixtures`, `data/samples/`). Never commit or
50:    print API keys.
51: 4. **No silent failures.** Validate inputs with the Zod schemas, throw clear errors, and never invent
52:    sources or evidence. Every finding needs a verbatim excerpt.
53: 5. **AI never decides.** Only a human sets `approved`, `rejected` or `deferred`. Every change to a
54:    requirement writes an AuditEvent.
55: 6. **Prove it works.** Add colocated `*.test.ts` files. Before you report done, run
56:    `npm run typecheck && npm test` from the repo root. For UI work, also run `npm run smoke` and look at
57:    the screenshots in `apps/desktop/out/smoke/`.
58: 7. **Respect the process split.** UI code (renderer) has no Node, no `fs` and no network. It talks to the
59:    main process only through `api` from `@/lib/api` (contract: `packages/core/src/ipc.ts`). Data, AI
60:    calls, files and API keys live in the main process. Build paths with `node:path` so they work on Windows.
61: 8. **Sessions are tracked with [Entire](https://github.com/entireio/cli).** Commit with plain `git`.
62:    Entire attaches your session to each commit as a checkpoint and pushes it on `git push`. Don't
63:    remove its hooks (`.claude/settings.json`, `.git/hooks`) and never put secrets in prompts.
64: 
65: 9. **Hand off in [docs/STATUS.md](docs/STATUS.md).** Claim your workstream there when you start; your
66:    tasks are the checklist in its section, in priority order. Update your own section (and only that
67:    one) when you finish a slice, get blocked or stop: tick done tasks, add a log entry. The next agent
68:    starts from it. The repo and Entire transcripts are **public**, so never paste keys or BMW data anywhere.
69: 
70: ## Commands (repo root, Node ≥ 22.13; works on Windows, macOS, Linux)
71: 
72: ```
73: npm install          # once
74: npm run dev          # opens the desktop app with hot reload
75: npm run smoke        # builds, screenshots every screen, checks the IPC bridge
76: npm test             # vitest, all packages
77: npm run typecheck    # all workspaces
78: npm run format       # prettier
79: npm run package      # installer for your OS → apps/desktop/release/
80: ```

(End of file - total 80 lines)
</content>

1: # ReqFlow — product definition
2: 
3: > Working name. One page, the source of truth for **what** we build. **How** is in
4: > [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md), **who builds what** in [docs/WORKSTREAMS.md](docs/WORKSTREAMS.md).
5: 
6: ## Problem
7: 
8: Defining the next generation of a BMW vehicle means working out what customers will value 3–5 years
9: from now. Today product managers do this by hand: they read customer feedback, BMW equipment and
10: sales data, customer studies and competitor and market information, then turn it into requirements.
11: It is slow, inconsistent and hard to trace. Months later nobody can say why a requirement exists,
12: what evidence backs it, or who decided it.
13: 
14: ## Product in one sentence
15: 
16: A visual, n8n-style **data flow** built from **building blocks** turns raw customer and market data into
17: **evidence-linked, prioritized car requirements**. A product manager reviews, challenges and decides on
18: them on the **Car** page, and every step is recorded in an **audit trail**.
19: 
20: > Customer requirement = customer-relevant attribute of a car. (BMW briefing)
21: 
22: ## Users
23: 
24: - **Product Manager (primary).** Owns the requirement set for one vehicle line × market. Makes every decision.
25: - **Analyst / PM ops (secondary).** Builds and tunes workflows, connects data and adjusts scoring in Settings.
26: 
27: ## The app — three tabs
28: 
29: A **native desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux**, not a web app. Everything runs locally on
30: the PM's machine. BMW files are imported through the system file dialog, results are exported
31: through the save dialog, and API keys are stored in the OS keychain. Only the AI and web-research
32: calls leave the machine. Layout (sketch: `context/Building_Blocks.jpeg`): the page fills the window, and
33: a tab bar at the bottom switches between **Data Flow · Car · Settings** (⌘/Ctrl + 1–3).
34: 
35: | Tab           | What the user does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
36: | ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
37: | **Data Flow** | **Building Blocks** on the left, the **Workplace** on the right. Drag blocks (or click them) onto the workplace, connect an output to an input, and set each block's parameters in the inspector. Custom, Research, AI Filter and AI Splitter blocks **expand** into their own inner workplace, built from the same blocks. Later: run the flow, see each block's status, counts and logs, and inspect what it produced. A run **pauses at HIL blocks** until a person has reviewed.                                                                                                                                                                              |
38: | **Car**       | The output: what the next car should offer. Today a placeholder (a car and the global vehicle/market). WS3 builds the requirement list here. Each requirement has an ID, title, description, measurable targets, category, score breakdown, priority with rationale, evidence level, assumptions, uncertainties, conflicting evidence and status, the agents' **confidence score** and a **Why?** link to their thought process, with a drill-down requirement → findings → verbatim evidence → source, **approve / reject / defer / edit / challenge** (rationale required) and the **audit trail**: who or what changed what, when, from what to what, and why. |
39: | **Settings**  | **App** (theme, workplace grid and minimap, delete confirmation) · **Global parameters** (vehicle line, derivative, code, market, horizon; prioritization weights and thresholds with a live example; output language) · **AI & research** (default provider and models; **API setups** for Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenAI-compatible servers and TypeSafe Jev, keys in the OS keychain, with a test button; which setup each Add to Car agent uses; web research, domains) · **Collaboration** (your name and role for the audit trail, team members and invitations, sharing via a shared folder or Git repo, notifications, four-eyes approval) · **About**.   |
40: 
41: ## The building blocks
42: 
43: Each block is specified as **Block (params / inner workplace / inputs / outputs)**, e.g. HIL (t/f/1/1)
44: = has parameters, no inner workplace, 1 input, 1 output. "n" = one port per entry of a list parameter.
45: Blocks are finalized one at a time; **State** says how far each one is.
46: 
47: | Block           | Spec         | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | State                                                                                                                        |
48: | --------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
49: | **Custom**      | (f/t/1/1)    | An empty block. Build any sub-flow inside it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | placeholder                                                                                                                  |
50: | **Raw**         | (t/f/0/1)    | Brings in Excel (.xlsx), CSV, Research JSON or a SQLite query as one unified data stream: one record per row (repeated feedback rows merged), report-style sheets read by section, plus usage findings from take rates and sales volumes. "Preview data" shows the parsed result right away.                                                                                                                                                                                   | **built**: .xlsx, CSV, JSON, SQLite; reads BMW's exports; runs in a flow once the executor exists (WS1)                      |
51: | **Research**    | (t/t/0/1)    | Searches the web; emits a data stream in the same format as Raw.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | placeholder params                                                                                                           |
52: | **AI Filter**   | (t/t/1/1)    | Keeps the items that match a criterion written in plain language.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | placeholder params                                                                                                           |
53: | **AI Splitter** | (t/t/1/2–10) | Routes each primary item while retaining linked evidence. Raw-data modes analyze customer demand into 2–10 bands, fixed car-part groups or custom global groups; legacy priority, category, sentiment and custom-instruction routing remain supported. An untouched inner workplace uses built-in routing; adding blocks or connections overrides it with a sub-flow.                                                                                                          | **built**: standalone Mastra Agent through the injected `LlmClient`, plus offline mock; report and paused-HIL routing review |
54: | **HIL**         | (t/f/1/1)    | Human in the loop (capacitor icon). The flow waits here until a person has reviewed what arrived, then passes it on. **Double-click opens the review report:** a flow chart of how the data was collected (every step it passed through, across inner workplaces) and a table icon on every step to see the data at that point.                                                                                                                                                | **finalized** — report and pause/continue logic built; runs once the executor exists (WS1)                                   |
55: | **Add to Car**  | (t/f/n/0)    | AI agents turn what arrives into requirements for the successor. Inputs **1. Priority … n. Priority** (the input an item arrives on sets its ranking) and **context inputs** (Auto, or Sales volumes) that are background only. Analysts, a synthesizer, an architect and a critic write and review each requirement; a judge rates it, and every requirement gets a **confidence score**. The block's **thought process** view shows, step by step, how the agents got there. | **built**: agents on any API setup from Settings, offline mock without a key; `npm run eval:f70`                             |
56: 
57: Spec and ports: `packages/core/src/blocks.ts`. Implementations: `packages/blocks/src/<block>/`.
58: 
59: Legacy splitter routing uses the most advanced populated layer (requirements, then themes, findings or
60: records) exactly once. Supporting evidence can appear on multiple branches. Unlinked upstream
61: context is retained on the first occupied branch and identified in the logs. Legacy priority routing
62: preserves existing priorities, including human overrides, otherwise calculates the weighted score
63: with Settings thresholds; missing factors remain provisional. Raw-data modes route original records
64: once and preserve their supporting context. Raw-data customer-priority analysis
65: consolidates needs across the full input and routes by demand bands (2–10); car-parts and custom
66: modes make a fixed global group plan. Demand frequency counts distinct expressed feedback units,
67: not unique customers or population prevalence. Its score weights normalized frequency 70% and
68: explicitly expressed supporting impact 30%; absent impact is NULL and means the demand score is not
69: computed. Context is not a vote; context and unscored records use the explicit lowest-band default,
70: not a claimed customer priority. Every assignment retains exact source-linked evidence, and analysis
71: does not invent sources or mutate human requirement decisions. A stored report supports transparent
72: review; while paused at an eligible HIL, a human may correct individual routes with rationale, with
73: the correction audited separately from scores and requirement decisions.
74: 
75: ## Default flow (template)
76: 
77: The default template mirrors the BMW process slide (`context/` image). The robot icon means the AI does the step on its own; the person icon means a human is involved.
78: 
79: ```
80: Situation analysis        Structure & context          Prioritization                  Review          Documentation
81: ──────────────────        ───────────────────          ──────────────                  ──────          ─────────────
82: Raw: customer feedback ┐
83: Raw: customer study    ┤
84: Raw: equipment data    ┼─▶ AI Filter ───────────────▶ AI Splitter ──must───▶ 🧑 HIL ──▶ 1. Priority ┐
85: Research: web          ┘   "customer-facing only"     "by priority" ──should─▶ 🧑 HIL ──▶ 2. Priority ┼─ Add to Car
86:                            (findings + evidence;       (explainable ──could──────────────▶ 3. Priority ┤  (agents: requirements
87:                            drops regulatory,           weighted       (unreviewed)                     │   with confidence and
88:                            engineering, pricing)       score)                                          │   a thought process)
89: Raw: sales volumes ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ Context 1   ┘
90:                                                                                           (Sales volumes: background only)
91: ```
92: 
93: **Where AI acts on its own:** ingestion (Raw, Research), filtering and extracting evidence-linked
94: findings (AI Filter), scoring and routing (AI Splitter), drafting, reviewing and rating requirements
95: (the Add to Car agents, each step visible in its thought-process view).
96: **Where a human must act:** at every HIL block, and when approving, rejecting, deferring or editing a
97: requirement, overriding a priority or answering a challenge on the Car tab. The AI can **never** set
98: a requirement to `approved` or `rejected`.
99: 
100: ## Core objects (full schemas in `packages/core`)
101: 
102: - **Source** — a dataset, document or web page, with a reliability rating.
103: - **SourceRecord** — one comment, row or paragraph from a source.
104: - **Finding** — a normalized signal (`complaint`, `unmet_need`, `praise`, `competitor_advantage`,
105:   `market_trend` or `usage_pattern`). It always cites ≥ 1 verbatim evidence excerpt.
106: - **Theme** — a cluster of duplicate or related findings.
107: - **Requirement** — `REQ-<vehicle>-<market>-<nnn>`. Holds the description, targets, linked findings and
108:   sources, score, priority with rationale, **evidence level A–D**, assumptions, uncertainties,
109:   conflicting findings and **status** (`proposed → in_review → approved | rejected | deferred`, plus
110:   `challenged`).
111: - **AuditEvent** — actor, action, entity, before/after changes, rationale and timestamp. Never edited or deleted.
112: 
113: ## Prioritization logic (explainable by design)
114: 
115: Six factors, each scored 0–5 with a one-line justification. On every factor, higher means "more worth doing":
116: customer impact · evidence strength · competitive gap · trend momentum (3–5 yr) · brand fit ·
117: ease (the inverse of rough effort/cost).
118: 
119: `score = 100 × Σ(weight × value) / (5 × Σ weight)`. The score maps to **must / should / could / won't**
120: using the thresholds set in Settings. The PM can override the priority, and the override is audited.
121: Evidence level is shown **next to** the score, never hidden inside it. A high score built on
122: D-level (assumption) evidence should catch the eye.
123: 
124: ## Evidence levels
125: 
126: **A** — several independent sources including quantitative BMW data · **B** — several sources, mostly
127: qualitative · **C** — a single source or anecdotal · **D** — rests mainly on forward-looking assumptions.
128: 
129: ## Scope rules (from the briefing)
130: 
131: - **In scope:** customer-facing attributes such as features, equipment, comfort, space, usability,
132:   infotainment and digital services, design and quality perception, driving experience, range and charging
133:   _as the customer experiences them_, and variants and packages.
134: - **Out of scope:** regulatory and homologation topics, technical and engineering specs, and
135:   pricing or business cases. An AI Filter removes these, and every exclusion is logged with a reason.
136: 
137: ## Demo scenario
138: 
139: **BMW 1 Series (F70) · EU · 5-year horizon**, because BMW's data is for the F70: customer feedback,
140: customer studies (the F70 next to the G60/G68 5 Series and G70 7 Series), sales volumes and the option
141: list. The requirements are for the F70's successor. This is the default scope in Settings.
142: 
143: 1. Open the default template, attach the BMW files to the Raw blocks, enable web research, and run.
144: 2. Watch the blocks fill up, then click the AI Filter to see findings with their evidence.
145: 3. The run pauses at the HIL block. On the Car tab, open a must-have and trace it down to a verbatim customer quote.
146: 4. Challenge one requirement. The AI answers. Edit one, approve one with a priority override, and reject one.
147: 5. Resume the run, which publishes and exports. The audit trail shows the full history of one requirement.
148: 6. Switch the scope to another series or market in Settings to show the workflow isn't a one-off.
149: 
150: ## Deliverables checklist (briefing → where we show it)
151: 
152: - [ ] Concept and working prototype → the app and this document
153: - [ ] Structured sample list of requirements with all the required fields → Car tab and export
154: - [ ] End-to-end workflow showing which steps the AI does alone and where a human must act → Data Flow tab (HIL blocks) and the diagram above
155: - [ ] Audit trail from source to decision → audit trail on the Car tab and the requirement History
156: 
157: ## Non-goals for the hackathon
158: 
159: Authentication, live multi-user editing and a sync server (Settings → Collaboration keeps the team and
160: the sharing choice on this computer; sending invitations and syncing come later, if at all), web and
161: mobile versions, signed installers and auto-update. Any of these can be mocked if the
162: demo needs them.

1: # Architecture
2: 
3: ReqFlow is a **native desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux** (Electron), not a web app.
4: Background and alternatives: [decisions/0002-electron-desktop-app.md](decisions/0002-electron-desktop-app.md).
5: Why the flow is built from blocks: [decisions/0003-building-blocks.md](decisions/0003-building-blocks.md).
6: 
7: ## Stack
8: 
9: | Concern         | Choice                                                                                | Why                                                                                                          |
10: | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
11: | Language        | TypeScript everywhere (npm workspaces)                                                | One shared contract for UI, engine and blocks                                                                |
12: | App shell       | Electron 44 (pinned, Node 24 inside), electron-vite 5, electron-builder               | Same Chromium on every OS; Node in the main process runs the engine                                          |
13: | UI              | React 19 + React Router (hash routing) + Tailwind 4 + zustand 5                       | Renders from `file://` in the installed app; small, testable stores                                          |
14: | Workflow canvas | `@xyflow/react` (React Flow 12)                                                       | The standard n8n-style node editor                                                                           |
15: | Schemas         | Zod 4                                                                                 | Runtime validation and TS types from one source                                                              |
16: | LLM             | Anthropic API and standalone Mastra Agent behind `LlmClient`, plus `mock`             | Swappable; works offline and in tests; Mastra is constructed per request without an attached Mastra instance |
17: | Persistence     | SQLite via built-in `node:sqlite`, in the OS app-data folder                          | Zero setup, no native module to rebuild per OS                                                               |
18: | Tests           | Vitest (colocated `*.test.ts`) + `npm run smoke` (clicks through the app in Electron) | Fast unit tests; a real-app check without clicking                                                           |
19: 
20: ## Repo layout
21: 
22: ```
23: .
24: ├── AGENTS.md  PRODUCT.md  README.md   ← start here
25: ├── context/                           ← original hackathon briefing + the app sketch (read-only)
26: ├── docs/                              ← ARCHITECTURE, WORKSTREAMS, STATUS, decisions/ (ADRs)
27: ├── data/
28: │   ├── raw/        (gitignored)       ← BMW-provided datasets
29: │   └── samples/                       ← small synthetic datasets for dev
30: ├── packages/
31: │   ├── core/       ← CONTRACT: domain schemas, blocks.ts (block specs), graph.ts (graph rules), IPC API, fixtures
32: │   ├── engine/     ← block contract + registry (done); executor (WS1)
33: │   ├── blocks/     ← block implementations, one folder per block + default template
34: │   ├── llm/        ← LlmClient implementations: anthropic, mock (WS7)
35: │   └── db/         ← SQLite repositories, AuditLogger, FileStore (WS1)
36: └── apps/desktop/                      ← the Electron app
37:     ├── electron.vite.config.ts  electron-builder.yml  build/ (icons)
38:     └── src/
39:         ├── main/       ← Node: window, IPC handlers, wiring of engine/db/llm, smoke test
40:         ├── preload/    ← the bridge: allow-listed invoke + run-update events (keep tiny)
41:         └── renderer/src/
42:             ├── pages/        DataflowPage · CarPage · SettingsPage
43:             ├── components/   dataflow/ (editor + its store) · settings/ · shell/ (bottom tabs) · ui/ (shared controls)
44:             ├── lib/          api.ts (the only way to main) · settings.ts (settings store) · theme.ts
45:             └── router.tsx  globals.css (design tokens, light + dark)
46: ```
47: 
48: Dependency direction (no cycles): `core ← engine ← blocks`, `core ← llm`, `core ← db`, and
49: `apps/desktop/src/main` → all of them. The renderer imports only `@reqflow/core` (types, block specs,
50: graph rules, fixtures). It never imports engine, db, llm or blocks.
51: 
52: ## Processes and security
53: 
54: ```
55: renderer (React, sandboxed)  ──api.x.y(…)──▶  preload (allow-list)  ──IPC──▶  main (Node)
56:    no Node, no fs, no network                                              engine · SQLite · LLM · files · keychain
57:            ◀──────────────── runs.onUpdate(run) push events ────────────────────────┘
58: ```
59: 
60: - `contextIsolation`, `sandbox` and no `nodeIntegration`. Production builds get a strict CSP
61:   (`connect-src 'self'`): all network calls (Claude, web search) happen in main.
62: - The preload only forwards channels listed in `IPC_INVOKE_METHODS`. Main also checks that the sender is the app window.
63: - The window never navigates away. `http(s)` links open in the user's browser.
64: - API keys are entered in Settings, encrypted with Electron `safeStorage` (OS keychain) and never sent to
65:   the renderer. In dev, `apps/desktop/.env` is also read (see `.env.example`).
66: 
67: ## The building blocks (`packages/core/src/blocks.ts`)
68: 
69: A workflow is a tree of **workplaces**. Each workplace holds blocks and edges. Seven kinds of block
70: are in the palette, defined once in `BLOCK_SPECS` (label, description, group, params, ports, whether
71: it has an inner workplace):
72: 
73: | Block       | Ports                                 | Inner workplace | Params (placeholders for now)                                                   |
74: | ----------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
75: | Custom      | 1 in · 1 out                          | yes             | none                                                                            |
76: | Raw         | no input · 1 out (data stream)        | no              | Excel/CSV/SQLite or Research JSON import, dataset, file/query                   |
77: | Research    | no input · 1 out (same format as Raw) | yes             | question, source types, market, age, results                                    |
78: | AI Filter   | 1 in · 1 out (kept)                   | yes             | criterion, model, min. confidence                                               |
79: | AI Splitter | 1 in · 2–10 outputs                   | yes             | customer priority, car parts, custom or legacy routing, branches, model         |
80: | HIL         | 1 in · 1 out                          | no              | reviewer, instructions, approvals, edits                                        |
81: | Add to Car  | one in **per priority** + context ins | no              | priorities, contexts (Auto / Sales volumes), max. requirements, vehicle, market |
82: 
83: - **Ports** come from `blockPorts(block)`. They can depend on params (the splitter's `branches`, Add to
84:   Car's `priorities` → `in-0` "1. Priority" … and `contexts` → `ctx-0` "Context 1 · Auto" …), and port
85:   ids are positional (`out-0`, `in-2`, `ctx-0`). Older flows are migrated on load (`migrateGraph`). When params change, `setBlockParams`
86:   removes edges on ports that no longer exist and returns them, so the editor can tell the user.
87: - **Params** are declared as `ParamSpec`s (text, textarea, number, slider, select, multiselect, toggle,
88:   list — free text, or one of `itemOptions` per entry — and file). The editor renders a form from them, and `parseBlockParams` validates strictly (unknown
89:   keys and wrong types are errors). Select options with the value `"global"` mean "use Settings →
90:   Global parameters".
91: - **Inner workplaces** (Custom, Research, AI Filter) hold a sub-flow built from the same blocks,
92:   recursively. Each one has fixed **boundary blocks**: one `block_input` per input port of the parent
93:   and one `block_output` per output port. They are created with the block and can't be deleted.
94: - **Ids** are unique across the whole tree, so run status and outputs are keyed by block id alone.
95: - **Graph rules** live in `packages/core/src/graph.ts` and are shared by the editor and the engine:
96:   `checkConnection` (ports exist, no self-loop, no duplicates, no cycles), `connect`, `removeBlocks`,
97:   `setBlockParams`, `graphAt` / `updateGraphAt` (navigate the tree), `validateGraph` (everything,
98:   recursively). Several edges may enter one input (merged) or leave one output (fan-out).
99: 
100: ## Add to Car agents
101: 
102: `packages/blocks/src/add-to-car/agents/`. Code does everything that must be exact; models read,
103: group, write and judge. One run of the block:
104: 
105: ```
106: context reader ─┐ (sales volumes summarized by code; Auto: a data profile the reader explains)
107: analysts (map) ─┴→ synthesizer (themes) → code picks themes → architect ⇄ critic → judge → code
108: ```
109: 
110: - **Analysts** read the priority inputs in batches (≤ 50 records, ≤ 14k chars, one input per batch)
111:   and return signals with record refs and quotes. Code checks every quote against the record
112:   (`findVerbatim`; a quote that isn't verbatim becomes the record's opening words) and turns signals
113:   into `Finding`s. Upstream findings are reused as they are.
114: - **Synthesizer** groups signals into themes (per category when there are many, then a merge pass).
115:   **Code** picks the themes: most important input first, then evidence weight (mentions ÷ rank);
116:   single comments and themes below `maxRequirements` are listed as held back, never dropped silently.
117: - **Architect** writes one requirement per theme from its strongest signals and the context briefs;
118:   the **critic** reviews it (accept / one rewrite / reject) and scores the six factors.
119: - **Judge** answers four typed questions (backed by evidence? customer-facing? still wanted at launch?
120:   testable?) through a `DecisionClient`: TypeSafe Jev (a "System 1" decision model with calibrated
121:   probabilities) or any LLM answering the same questions.
122: - **Code** assigns ids, priority from the input rank (first third of n inputs must, then should,
123:   then could), the critic's weighted score, evidence level A–D, and the confidence: a weighted
124:   geometric mean of the judge's answers, evidence breadth, the critic's verdict and conflicts.
125: - Everything is recorded in a `ReasoningTrace` (`packages/core/src/reasoning.ts`), stored by run and
126:   block (`reasoning_traces`) and shown in the thought-process view (block button, inspector, Car → Why?).
127: - Each role runs on an API setup (Settings → AI → Agents; `apps/desktop/src/main/agents.ts`). Providers
128:   live in `packages/llm`: Claude (adaptive thinking by effort, summarized thinking kept for the trace),
129:   OpenAI / Gemini / OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions, TypeSafe Jev, and the offline mock, which runs
130:   the same pipeline by rules and marks everything "[Offline]".
131: - `npm run eval:f70` runs the agents on BMW's F70 files with the user's setups and prints numbers only;
132:   the full output goes to `data/raw/eval/` (gitignored).
133: 
134: ## Data flow: one envelope per port
135: 
136: Every port carries a `PipelineData` envelope (`sources, records, findings, themes, requirements`).
137: Raw and Research emit sources and records (the "unified data stream"). Raw accepts Excel, CSV,
138: read-only SQLite queries, and declared Research JSON envelopes. JSON import validates core schemas
139: and references but preserves the original objects, extensions, provenance and envelope metadata;
140: it rejects duplicate identities and dangling evidence rather than dropping them. Later blocks enrich the same
141: envelope: AI Filter keeps matching items (and extracts evidence-linked findings), AI Splitter routes
142: items to one branch each, HIL passes on what the reviewer approved, and Add to Car's agents turn what
143: arrives on its priority inputs into requirements (the input it arrives on sets the ranking; context
144: inputs are background only, see "Add to Car agents"). Several edges into one input are combined
145: with `mergePipelineData` (concatenate, de-duplicate by `id`, later edge wins).
146: 
147: ```ts
148: defineBlock({
149:   kind: "ai_filter",
150:   async run(inputs, params, ctx) {
151:     const input = inputs.in; // one envelope per input port id
152:     /* ctx.llm, ctx.audit, ctx.log … */
153:     return { status: "ok", outputs: { out: kept } }; // one envelope per output port id
154:   },
155: });
156: ```
157: 
158: ## Engine semantics (WS1 implements, everyone relies on)
159: 
160: 1. **Validate before running** with `validateGraph`, and check that every block kind (except
161:    Custom) has an implementation (`BlockRegistry.missing()`). If anything fails, the run fails before it
162:    starts, with per-block errors.
163: 2. **Execute each workplace in topological order.** A block's input per port is the merge of what its
164:    incoming edges carry. Store each block's output per port and push `BlockRun` status, counts, logs,
165:    progress and any analytical splitter report snapshot via `runs.onUpdate`.
166: 3. **Inner workplaces.** A block whose inner workplace contains blocks runs that sub-flow: each
167:    `block_input` emits what arrived on its parent port, and what reaches each `block_output` becomes
168:    the parent's output on that port. A Custom block always runs its sub-flow. Research and AI Filter run
169:    their built-in implementation while their inner workplace is empty.
170: 4. **Failure.** A block that throws is marked `failed`, its downstream blocks `skipped`, and the run
171:    `failed`. Nothing is partially published.
172: 5. **Pause / resume.** HIL returns `{ status: "paused" }` → the run is `waiting_for_review`.
173:    `runs.resume` reloads what the reviewer changed, re-invokes the block with `ctx.resumed = true`, and continues.
174: 6. **Cancel.** The run's `AbortSignal` fires, and blocks must stop promptly.
175: 7. **Audit.** The engine logs `run.*` events, blocks log what they create or change, and handlers log human actions.
176: 
177: ## IPC API (`packages/core/src/ipc.ts`)
178: 
179: UI code calls `api.<namespace>.<method>(…)` from `@/lib/api`. Main implements `ReqflowHandlers`
180: (`apps/desktop/src/main/handlers.ts`). Failures arrive as `ReqflowError` with a `code`
181: (`invalid_input`, `not_found`, `not_implemented`, `internal`, …). Arguments must be plain data. Main
182: validates every argument with the Zod schemas, because the renderer counts as untrusted input.
183: 
184: | Method                                               | Purpose                                                                                                                                   |
185: | ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
186: | `app.info()`                                         | Version, OS, data directory (**built**)                                                                                                   |
187: | `templates.list()`                                   | Workflow templates (`BMW_DEFAULT_TEMPLATE`) (**built**)                                                                                   |
188: | `workflows.list/get/save/remove`                     | Workflow CRUD. `save` assigns the id and bumps `version`                                                                                  |
189: | `blocks.preview(request)`                            | Runs a block without inputs (Raw) on its own and returns its output and log (**built**)                                                   |
190: | `files.import()`                                     | Native open dialog → copies the file into the data dir → `StoredFileInfo` (`null` if cancelled). Raw's `file` param stores it (**built**) |
191: | `runs.start/get/list/blockOutput/resume/cancel`      | Run lifecycle. `blockOutput` returns that block's output per port                                                                         |
192: | `runs.onUpdate(listener)`                            | Push events on every status, progress or log change (no polling)                                                                          |
193: | `requirements.list(filter)` · `requirements.get(id)` | Latest versions · `RequirementDetail` (findings, evidence, sources, versions)                                                             |
194: | `requirements.edit(id, RequirementEdit)`             | PM edit, rationale required → new version and audit                                                                                       |
195: | `requirements.decide(id, RequirementDecision)`       | Approve / reject / defer / challenge / reopen. A challenge makes the AI answer (`challenge_answered`) and returns it to `in_review`       |
196: | `requirements.reset()`                               | Removes every requirement (Car page → Reset). Writes one `requirement.deleted` audit event each; ids are never reused                     |
197: | `audit.list(filter)`                                 | Audit events, ascending by time                                                                                                           |
198: | `settings.get/save` · `settings.secrets/setSecret`   | `Settings` (save logs `settings.changed` with a diff) · API-key status / store a key in the keychain                                      |
199: | `exports.requirements({ runId, format })`            | Native save dialog → JSON / CSV / Markdown (logs `export.created`)                                                                        |
200: 
201: To add a method: add it to `ReqflowApi` **and** `IPC_INVOKE_METHODS` (the compiler enforces both),
202: then implement it in `handlers.ts`.
203: 
204: ## HIL review report
205: 
206: Double-clicking a HIL block (or its report icon) opens `components/dataflow/report/HilReport.tsx`:
207: 
208: - **Flow chart** from `traceLineage(root, path, blockId)` (`packages/core/src/lineage.ts`): every step
209:   data passes through on its way into the block. It leaves inner workplaces through their
210:   `block_input` and traces through the sub-flow of upstream blocks that have blocks inside.
211: - **Data at a step** (table icon on every step; the HIL itself = "data at this point"). Steps without
212:   inputs (Raw) show their **real data** via `blocks.preview`, and so does a HIL fed directly by them.
213:   After a run it shows `api.runs.blockOutput()` of the step (for the HIL: the merge of what its
214:   incoming edges carried). Otherwise it says nothing has arrived yet; there is no demo data.
215: - At run time the HIL block (`packages/blocks/src/hil/hil.ts`) pauses the run until the review is done
216:   and then passes the data on unchanged; edits go through the requirement API (audited).
217: 
218: ## AI Splitter: raw analysis and review
219: 
220: The raw-data splitter uses a standalone Mastra `Agent` behind the existing injected `LlmClient`.
221: It receives the run's model configuration and secret-store API key; the Agent is not attached to a
222: Mastra instance, tools, storage, memory or tracing. Structured requests use strict Zod validation,
223: one generation step and no retries. Tests can inject the Agent factory, while production defaults
224: to the standalone implementation. Legacy `priority`, `category`, `sentiment` and `custom` routing
225: modes remain available alongside raw-data `customer_priority`, `car_parts` and `custom` analysis.
226: 
227: Raw analysis discovers candidate needs in batches of at most 20 records, consolidates them globally,
228: then assigns against the consolidated catalog. Car-part/custom modes create exactly the configured
229: 2–10 global groups before assignment; customer-priority mode uses canonical needs and creates 2–10
230: demand bands. Oversized prompts fail explicitly rather than truncating evidence. Code verifies
231: complete item/need coverage and each cited source, record, locator and verbatim excerpt. The model
232: does not return scores, unit IDs, routes or human decisions.
233: 
234: Demand counts distinct expressed feedback units, not unique customers or population prevalence;
235: customer count is unknown. Explicit original/provider identities and reimport evidence can deduplicate
236: units, while distinct record/customer identities remain independent even if their text matches.
237: Sales, equipment and other context are not votes. Frequency is the share of supporting feedback units
238: relative to the highest-supporting global group and is weighted 70%; mean explicitly expressed
239: supporting impact is weighted 30%. An absent impact anchor is `NULL`, not zero; without available
240: impact or supporting feedback, the score is `NULL`. Opposing and unclear evidence remains visible,
241: and confidence is not demand. Output retains a versioned analytical report with score method, group
242: scores, item assignments, evidence, source matrix, limitations and human review history. The report
243: is stored with the `BlockRun` snapshot and rendered as score, evidence-balance and source-by-group
244: graphics with exact evidence drill-down.
245: 
246: At a paused eligible HIL, a reviewer may correct individual item routes with a required rationale.
247: Corrections update the run's routing report and audit history; computed scores and original evidence
248: remain unchanged. The review is available only while the upstream splitter is behind the current
249: paused HIL with reviewer edits enabled. It never edits or decides a requirement; requirement
250: approval, rejection or deferral remains a separate human action on the Car page.
251: 
252: ## Renderer state
253: 
254: - **`components/dataflow/store.ts`**: the editor store (zustand). It holds the workflow tree, the
255:   open workplace (`path`), the selection, React Flow sizes and a notice. Every edit goes through the
256:   core graph rules; errors become a visible notice, never a silent no-op. It lives for the whole app
257:   session, so switching tabs keeps the flow. It isn't saved to disk yet (`workflows.*` is WS1).
258: - **`lib/settings.ts`**: the settings store. It loads `settings.get()` at startup, validates every
259:   change with the `Settings` schema and saves in the background. While main has no settings storage
260:   (`not_implemented`), it keeps the defaults and the Settings page says so.
261: - **zustand 5 rule:** never return a new object or array from a selector (it re-renders forever).
262:   Select existing objects or primitives and derive the rest with `useMemo`.
263: - **Theme:** `lib/theme.ts` sets `<html data-theme>` from Settings (system, light or dark). The CSS
264:   tokens in `globals.css` follow it, so use token classes (`bg-panel`, `text-muted`, …), never hex colors.
265: - **Colorway: BMW M.** The M stripe colours (`m-light` #81C4FF, `m-dark` #16588E, `m-red` #E7222E) on
266:   carbon neutrals. Block groups take them: sources light blue, AI dark blue, HIL red (a person has to
267:   act), Add to Car neutral. `MStripe` (`components/ui/`) marks the active tab. Filled controls use
268:   `bg-brand-fill` so white text stays readable in both themes.
269: 
270: ## AI usage rules
271: 
272: - Use `ctx.llm.generateObject` with a Zod schema for every AI step. Invalid output → throw.
273: - **Never trust model-cited evidence.** The model returns `recordId` and `excerpt`. Code checks that
274:   the excerpt is a verbatim substring of that record, and drops or flags the finding if it isn't.
275: - Batch the records. Use `tier: "fast"` for per-record extraction and `default` for clustering, derivation and challenges.
276: - AI actors in the audit trail record the exact model id returned by the client.
277: - The `mock` provider must return schema-valid, deterministic output so the whole pipeline runs offline.
278: - Prompts live next to the block that uses them (`blocks/src/<block>/<name>.prompt.ts`).
279: 
280: ## Persistence notes (WS1)
281: 
282: - The database lives in the per-user app-data folder (`main/paths.ts`: macOS
283:   `~/Library/Application Support/ReqFlow/data`, Windows `%APPDATA%\ReqFlow\data`, Linux
284:   `~/.config/ReqFlow/data`). `REQFLOW_DATA_DIR` overrides it. Always build paths with `node:path`, never
285:   with string concatenation (Windows uses `\`).
286: - Only one app instance runs at a time (single-instance lock), so only one process writes SQLite.
287: - Workflows are stored whole (the block tree as JSON) and versioned on save.
288: - Requirements are versioned: one row per `(id, version)`. "Current" means the max version.
289: - `audit_events` is insert-only, with no update or delete code path.
290: - Block outputs are stored per `(runId, blockId, port)` as JSON. Imported files are copied into `uploads/`
291:   inside the data dir by the file store (`packages/db/src/files.ts`, built), metadata next to each file.
292: 
293: ## Running, checking, packaging
294: 
295: | Command (repo root) | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
296: | ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
297: | `npm run dev`       | Opens the app with hot reload (renderer) and auto-restart (main)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
298: | `npm run smoke`     | Builds, then drives the real app off screen: opens every screen, adds every block, opens an inner workplace, types into fields, connects ports by mouse drag (and checks a loop is refused), walks the settings, switches to dark mode, screenshots each step to `apps/desktop/out/smoke/`, checks the IPC bridge, and exits non-zero on any failed check or renderer error |
299: | `npm run check`     | Typecheck + unit tests + format check                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
300: | `npm run package`   | Installer for the **current** OS in `apps/desktop/release/`: `.exe` (NSIS), `.dmg` or `.AppImage`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

3: Each workstream (WS) owns a set of paths, so parallel agents never edit the same files. Everything
4: builds against the contract in `packages/core` (block specs in `blocks.ts`, graph rules in `graph.ts`)
5: and the block contract in `packages/engine/src/block.ts`. UI workstreams use `@reqflow/core/fixtures`

13: and "done when".

28: with a merge commit, never a squash, so Entire's checkpoint trailers survive. To add a dependency, add it to **your own** package's

1: import readXlsxFile from "read-excel-file/node";
2: import { decodeText, parseCsv } from "./csv";
3: import type { Cell } from "./table";
4: 
5: export interface ReadResult {
6:   rows: Cell[][];
7:   sheet?: string; // the sheet that was read (Excel only)
8:   notes: string[];
9: }
10: 
11: const isZip = (b: Uint8Array) => b[0] === 0x50 && b[1] === 0x4b && b[2] === 0x03 && b[3] === 0x04;
12: const isOle = (b: Uint8Array) => b[0] === 0xd0 && b[1] === 0xcf && b[2] === 0x11 && b[3] === 0xe0;
13: const isPdf = (b: Uint8Array) => b[0] === 0x25 && b[1] === 0x50 && b[2] === 0x44 && b[3] === 0x46; // %PDF
14: 
15: /**
16:  * Reads an uploaded file into raw rows. The format is decided by its content, not its name:
17:  * `.xlsx` (zip) via read-excel-file, legacy `.xls` and PDFs are refused with a fix, anything else is
18:  * CSV text.
19:  */
20: export async function readSpreadsheet(
21:   name: string,
22:   bytes: Uint8Array,
23:   sheet: string,
24: ): Promise<ReadResult> {
25:   if (isOle(bytes) || /\.xls$/i.test(name)) {
26:     throw new Error(
27:       `"${name}" is an old .xls file. Open it in Excel and save it as .xlsx or .csv.`,
28:     );
29:   }
30:   if (isPdf(bytes) || /\.pdf$/i.test(name)) {
31:     throw new Error(
32:       `"${name}" is a PDF. The Raw block reads tables from Excel (.xlsx) or CSV files; PDFs aren't supported yet.`,
33:     );
34:   }
35:   if (isZip(bytes)) {
36:     let sheets: { sheet: string; data: unknown[][] }[];
37:     try {
38:       sheets = await readXlsxFile(Buffer.from(bytes));
39:     } catch (err) {
40:       throw new Error(
41:         `"${name}" couldn't be read as an Excel file: ${err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)}`,
42:       );
43:     }
44:     if (sheets.length === 0) throw new Error(`"${name}" has no sheets`);
45:     const wanted = sheet.trim();
46:     const picked = wanted
47:       ? sheets.find((s) => s.sheet.toLowerCase() === wanted.toLowerCase())
48:       : sheets[0];
49:     if (!picked) {
50:       throw new Error(
51:         `"${name}" has no sheet "${wanted}". Sheets: ${sheets.map((s) => `"${s.sheet}"`).join(", ")}`,
52:       );
53:     }
54:     const notes =
55:       !wanted && sheets.length > 1
56:         ? [`Read the first of ${sheets.length} sheets ("${picked.sheet}").`]
57:         : [];
58:     return { rows: picked.data as Cell[][], sheet: picked.sheet, notes };
59:   }
60:   const notes = sheet.trim()
61:     ? [`"${name}" is a CSV file, so the sheet name "${sheet}" was ignored.`]
62:     : [];
63:   return { rows: parseCsv(decodeText(bytes)), notes };
64: }

41: const textLength = (table: Table, col: number) => {
42:   const texts = table.rows.map((r) => cellText(r.cells[col] ?? null)).filter(Boolean);

50: export function textColumn(table: Table): number {
51:   const candidates = findColumns(table.header, "text");
52:   if (candidates.length <= 1) return candidates[0] ?? -1;
53:   return candidates.reduce((best, c) =>
54:     textLength(table, c) > textLength(table, best) ? c : best,
55:   );

58: /** The market column, preferring codes ("EU", "GB") over names ("Europe") when both are there. */
59: export function marketColumn(table: Table): number {
60:   const candidates = findColumns(table.header, "market");
61:   const isCodes = (col: number) =>
62:     table.rows.every((r) => {
63:       const v = cellText(r.cells[col] ?? null);
64:       return !v || /^[A-Za-z]{2,3}$/.test(v);
65:     });
66:   return candidates.find(isCodes) ?? candidates[0] ?? -1;
67: }

69: /** Numbers in record text: at most 4 decimals ("0.8123" instead of "0.81234567891234"). */

73: /** "rows 3–5" for a run of rows, otherwise "rows 3, 7, 9". */
74: function rowRange(lines: number[]): string {
75:   if (lines.length === 1) return `row ${lines[0]}`;
76:   const contiguous = lines.every((l, i) => i === 0 || l === lines[i - 1]! + 1);

80: /** A column's value across merged rows: the value when they agree, else the distinct values. */
81: function mergedValue(rows: TableRow[], col: number): unknown {
82:   const values: unknown[] = [];
83:   const seen = new Set<string>();
84:   for (const row of rows) {
85:     const c = row.cells[col] ?? null;
86:     if (c === null) continue;
87:     const v = c instanceof Date ? cellText(c) : c;
88:     if (!seen.has(String(v))) {
89:       seen.add(String(v));
90:       values.push(v);
91:     }
92:   }
93:   return values.length === 0 ? null : values.length === 1 ? values[0] : values;
94: }

98:  * Exports that repeat a comment on several rows, once per classification, are merged back into

100:  */
101: export function tableToRecords(table: Table, o: IngestOptions): Ingested {
102:   const notes: string[] = [];
103:   const sourceId = `src_${shortHash(o.key)}`;

108:   const languageCol = findColumns(table.header, "language")[0] ?? -1;
109: 
110:   if (isText && textCol === -1) {
111:     notes.push(

114:   }
115: 
116:   const textOfRow = (row: TableRow) =>
117:     textCol !== -1

121:           .filter((part): part is string => part !== null)
122:           .join("; ");
123: 
124:   // Group the rows that become one record, in order of first appearance.
125:   const groups: { text: string; rows: TableRow[]; indexes: number[] }[] = [];
126:   const byKey = new Map<string, (typeof groups)[number]>();
127:   const noText: number[] = [];
128:   table.rows.forEach((row, i) => {
129:     const text = textOfRow(row);
130:     if (!text.trim()) {
131:       noText.push(row.line);
132:       return;
133:     }
134:     const id = idCol !== -1 ? cellText(row.cells[idCol] ?? null) : "";
135:     const key = id ? `${id}\u0000${text}` : null;
136:     const existing = key ? byKey.get(key) : undefined;
137:     if (existing) {
138:       existing.rows.push(row);
139:       existing.indexes.push(i);
140:       return;
141:     }
142:     const group = { text, rows: [row], indexes: [i] };
143:     groups.push(group);
144:     if (key) byKey.set(key, group);
145:   });
146:   if (noText.length)

149:   const merged = groups.filter((g) => g.rows.length > 1);
150:   if (merged.length) {

152:       merged.some((g) => Array.isArray(mergedValue(g.rows, j))),
153:     );

156:         (varying.length

159:     );
160:   }

166:     }

172:     }
173:   }

192:       market: market || o.scope.market,

69: interface TextFragment {
70:   str: string;
71:   x: number;
72:   y: number;
73:   width: number;
74:   height: number;
75: }
76: 
77: function assemblePageText(fragments: TextFragment[]): string {
78:   if (fragments.length === 0) return "";
79: 
80:   // Sort fragments by y descending (top to bottom in PDF coordinate space)
81:   const sorted = [...fragments].sort((a, b) => {
82:     const dy = b.y - a.y;
83:     if (Math.abs(dy) > 3) return dy;
84:     return a.x - b.x;
85:   });
86: 
87:   const lines: TextFragment[][] = [];
88:   for (const frag of sorted) {
89:     const line = lines.find((l) => {
90:       const lineY = l[0]!.y;
91:       const tol = Math.max(frag.height * 0.5, 3);
92:       return Math.abs(frag.y - lineY) <= tol;
93:     });
94: 
95:     if (line) {
96:       line.push(frag);
97:     } else {
98:       lines.push([frag]);
99:     }
100:   }
101: 
102:   // Sort lines top-to-bottom
103:   lines.sort((a, b) => b[0]!.y - a[0]!.y);
104: 
105:   const lineStrings: string[] = [];
106:   for (const line of lines) {
107:     line.sort((a, b) => a.x - b.x);
108:     let lineStr = "";
109:     for (const f of line) {
110:       const cleanStr = f.str.replace(/[\u0000-\u0008\u000B\u000C\u000E-\u001F]/g, " ");
111:       if (!cleanStr) continue;
112:       if (!lineStr) {
113:         lineStr = cleanStr;
114:       } else {
115:         const needsSpace = !lineStr.endsWith(" ") && !cleanStr.startsWith(" ");
116:         lineStr += (needsSpace ? " " : "") + cleanStr;
117:       }
118:     }
119:     const trimmed = lineStr.replace(/[ \t]+/g, " ").trimEnd();
120:     if (trimmed) {
121:       lineStrings.push(trimmed);
122:     }
123:   }
124: 
125:   return lineStrings.join("\n");
126: }

128: export async function readPdf(
129:   name: string,
130:   bytes: Uint8Array,
131:   options: ReadPdfOptions = {},
132: ): Promise<ReadPdfOutput> {
133:   if (bytes.byteLength > MAX_FILE_SIZE_BYTES) {
134:     throw new Error(
135:       `"${name}" exceeds the maximum PDF size limit of 30MB (${(bytes.byteLength / (1024 * 1024)).toFixed(1)}MB).`,
136:     );
137:   }
138: 
139:   if (!isPdfMagic(bytes)) {
140:     throw new Error(`"${name}" is not a valid PDF file.`);
141:   }
142: 
143:   // Ensure Node globals exist before importing pdfjs
144:   const canvasModule = await import("@napi-rs/canvas");
145:   const g = globalThis as unknown as Record<string, unknown>;
146:   if (typeof g.DOMMatrix === "undefined" && canvasModule.DOMMatrix) {
147:     g.DOMMatrix = canvasModule.DOMMatrix;
148:   }
149:   if (typeof g.ImageData === "undefined" && canvasModule.ImageData) {
150:     g.ImageData = canvasModule.ImageData;
151:   }
152:   if (typeof g.Path2D === "undefined" && canvasModule.Path2D) {
153:     g.Path2D = canvasModule.Path2D;
154:   }
155:   if (typeof g.Image === "undefined" && canvasModule.Image) {
156:     g.Image = canvasModule.Image;
157:   }
158: 
159:   // Dynamically import pdfjs
160:   const pdfjs = await import("pdfjs-dist/legacy/build/pdf.mjs");
161:   const workerSrc = require.resolve("pdfjs-dist/legacy/build/pdf.worker.mjs");
162:   pdfjs.GlobalWorkerOptions.workerSrc = workerSrc;
163: 
164:   const loadingTask = pdfjs.getDocument({
165:     data: bytes,
166:     disableFontFace: true,
167:     enableXfa: false,
168:     useSystemFonts: false,
169:     ...( { isEvalSupported: false } as any ),
170:   });
171: 
172:   if (options.signal) {
173:     options.signal.addEventListener("abort", () => loadingTask.destroy(), { once: true });
174:     options.signal.throwIfAborted();
175:   }
176: 
177:   let doc;
178:   try {
179:     doc = await loadingTask.promise;
180:   } catch (err) {
181:     if (options.signal?.aborted) throw options.signal.reason;
182:     throw new Error(
183:       `"${name}" could not be parsed as a PDF: ${err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)}`,
184:     );
185:   }
186: 
187:   if (doc.numPages > MAX_PDF_PAGES) {
188:     await doc.cleanup();
189:     await loadingTask.destroy();
190:     throw new Error(
191:       `"${name}" has ${doc.numPages} pages, exceeding the maximum limit of ${MAX_PDF_PAGES} pages.`,
192:     );
193:   }
194: 
195:   const pages: PdfPageResult[] = [];
196:   const notes: string[] = [];
197:   let ocrWorker: any = null;
198: 
199:   const getOcrWorker = async () => {
200:     if (ocrWorker) return ocrWorker;
201:     const { createWorker } = await import("tesseract.js");
202:     const workerPath = require.resolve("tesseract.js/src/worker-script/node/index.js");
203:     const corePath = require.resolve("tesseract.js-core");
204:     const langDir = getTessLangDir();
205: 
206:     ocrWorker = await createWorker(["eng", "deu"], 1, {
207:       workerPath,
208:       corePath,
209:       langPath: langDir,
210:       gzip: true,
211:       cacheMethod: "none",
212:       logger: () => {},
213:     });
214:     return ocrWorker;
215:   };
216: 
217:   try {
218:     for (let pageNum = 1; pageNum <= doc.numPages; pageNum++) {
219:       options.signal?.throwIfAborted();
220: 
221:       const page = await doc.getPage(pageNum);
222:       const textContent = await page.getTextContent({ includeMarkedContent: false });
223: 
224:       const fragments: TextFragment[] = [];
225:       for (const item of textContent.items) {
226:         if ("str" in item && typeof item.str === "string" && item.str.length > 0) {
227:           fragments.push({
228:             str: item.str,
229:             x: item.transform[4] ?? 0,
230:             y: item.transform[5] ?? 0,
231:             width: item.width ?? 0,
232:             height: item.height ?? 0,
233:           });
234:         }
235:       }
236: 
237:       let extractedText = assemblePageText(fragments);
238:       if (extractedText.length > MAX_PAGE_CHARS) {
239:         throw new Error(
240:           `Page ${pageNum} of "${name}" exceeds the maximum characters limit of ${MAX_PAGE_CHARS} (${extractedText.length} chars).`,
241:         );
242:       }
243: 
244:       const trimmedText = extractedText.trim();
245:       const isSparseOrEmpty = trimmedText.length < OCR_SPARSE_THRESHOLD_CHARS;
246: 
247:       if (!isSparseOrEmpty) {
248:         pages.push({
249:           page: pageNum,
250:           text: extractedText,
251:           method: "text",
252:         });
253:         continue;
254:       }
255: 
256:       // Page is sparse or empty: attempt local OCR
257:       const baseViewport = page.getViewport({ scale: 1.0 });
258:       if (baseViewport.width * baseViewport.height > MAX_RENDER_PIXELS) {
259:         throw new Error(
260:           `Page ${pageNum} render resolution (${Math.round(baseViewport.width * baseViewport.height)} pixels) exceeds limit of 8M pixels.`,
261:         );
262:       }
263: 
264:       const maxScale = Math.sqrt(MAX_RENDER_PIXELS / (baseViewport.width * baseViewport.height));
265:       const scale = Math.min(2.0, maxScale);
266:       const viewport = page.getViewport({ scale });
267: 
268:       if (viewport.width * viewport.height > MAX_RENDER_PIXELS) {
269:         throw new Error(`Page ${pageNum} render resolution exceeds limit of 8M pixels.`);
270:       }
271: 
272:       const canvas = canvasModule.createCanvas(
273:         Math.floor(viewport.width),
274:         Math.floor(viewport.height),
275:       );
276:       const context = canvas.getContext("2d");
277: 
278:       const renderTask = page.render({
279:         canvas: null,
280:         canvasContext: context as any,
281:         viewport,
282:       });
283:       if (options.signal) {
284:         options.signal.addEventListener("abort", () => renderTask.cancel(), { once: true });
285:       }
286: 
287:       await renderTask.promise;
288:       const imageBuffer = canvas.toBuffer("image/png");
289: 
290:       const worker = await getOcrWorker();
291:       options.signal?.throwIfAborted();
292: 
293:       let ocrRecognizePromise: Promise<any> = worker.recognize(imageBuffer);
294:       let timer: NodeJS.Timeout | null = null;
295:       const timeoutPromise = new Promise((_, reject) => {
296:         timer = setTimeout(
297:           () => reject(new Error(`OCR timeout on page ${pageNum} after ${OCR_PAGE_TIMEOUT_MS}ms`)),
298:           OCR_PAGE_TIMEOUT_MS,
299:         );
300:       });
301: 
302:       let ocrResult: any;
303:       try {
304:         ocrResult = await Promise.race([ocrRecognizePromise, timeoutPromise]);
305:       } finally {
306:         if (timer) clearTimeout(timer);
307:       }
308: 
309:       const ocrText = (ocrResult?.data?.text ?? "").trim();
310:       const ocrConfidence =
311:         typeof ocrResult?.data?.confidence === "number" ? ocrResult.data.confidence : undefined;
312: 
313:       if (ocrText.length > MAX_PAGE_CHARS) {
314:         throw new Error(
315:           `Page ${pageNum} OCR text of "${name}" exceeds limit of ${MAX_PAGE_CHARS} chars.`,
316:         );
317:       }
318: 
319:       if (ocrText.length > 0) {
320:         pages.push({
321:           page: pageNum,
322:           text: ocrText,
323:           method: "ocr",
324:           confidence: ocrConfidence,
325:         });
326:         if (options.log) {
327:           options.log(`Page ${pageNum}: OCR extracted ${ocrText.length} characters.`);
328:         }
329:       } else if (trimmedText.length > 0) {
330:         // Preserve nonempty sparse text if OCR yields none
331:         pages.push({
332:           page: pageNum,
333:           text: extractedText,
334:           method: "text",
335:         });
336:       } else {
337:         // Blank page: report rather than skipping silently
338:         pages.push({
339:           page: pageNum,
340:           text: "",
341:           method: "ocr",
342:           confidence: ocrConfidence,
343:         });
344:         notes.push(`Page ${pageNum} is blank.`);
345:         if (options.log) {
346:           options.log(`Page ${pageNum} is blank.`);
347:         }
348:       }
349:     }
350:   } finally {
351:     if (ocrWorker) {
352:       try {
353:         await ocrWorker.terminate();
354:       } catch {
355:         // ignore termination errors
356:       }
357:       ocrWorker = null;
358:     }
359:     if (doc) {
360:       await doc.cleanup();
361:       await loadingTask.destroy();
362:     }
363:   }
364: 
365:   return { pages, notes };

1: # Sample datasets (synthetic)
2: 
3: **Invented for development and tests. Not BMW data, not real customer quotes.** Real BMW files go in
4: `data/raw/`, which is gitignored.
5: 
6: Regenerate them with `node data/samples/generate.ts` (Node ≥ 23.6). They imitate what BMW exports
7: might look like, including the awkward parts the Raw block has to handle:
8: 
9: | File                       | Raw block "Dataset" | Format                                                                                                  | What the Raw block makes of it                                                                                                  |
10: | -------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
11: | `customer_feedback.csv`    | Customer feedback   | UTF-8 with BOM, `,`, quoted comments with commas, quotes and a line break; de/en/fr/it/es               | 35 records (one per comment, language and market per row); the row without a comment is skipped and reported                   |
12: | `equipment_take_rates.csv` | Equipment data      | German Excel export: `;`, decimal commas, Windows-1252, German headers (`Ausstattung`, `Einbaurate %`) | 17 records; 8 usage findings (take rate ≥ 70 % → expected as standard, ≤ 15 % → rarely chosen); the row without a rate is reported |
13: | `sales_volumes.csv`        | Sales volumes       | `,`, one row per derivative and year                                                                    | 12 records; 2 findings (volume change ≥ 10 % between first and last year); the i5 Touring launch (0 units in 2023) is noted        |
14: | `customer_study.xlsx`      | Customer study      | Excel workbook with two sheets: `Results` (scores) and `Verbatims` (free text)                          | Sheet empty → first sheet (7 records); sheet `Verbatims` → 6 records with languages                                             |
15: 
16: How columns are recognised (English and German names): `packages/blocks/src/raw/columns.ts`.
17: 
18: BMW's real files stay in `data/raw/` (gitignored). When they're there, `npm test` also runs the
19: "BMW …" suites in `packages/blocks/src/raw/raw.test.ts` (structure checks only) and `npm run smoke`
20: previews them in the app. To try them by hand: `npm run dev`, add a Raw block, choose the file.
